segments.title: Four books for approaching medieval warfare
segments.summary: The medieval-themed reading list opens with Montgomery's illustrated survey of warfare and its maps of major campaigns.
segments.body: Four books approach medieval conflict through Norman warfare, crusading, the Mediterranean world, and Anglo-French rivalry. Bernard Montgomery's A Concise History of Warfare opens the selection. The copy shown is a 2000 Wordsworth edition of a book published by William Collins and Sons in 1968. Its black-and-white presentation is plain, but its maps and broad campaign coverage make it a practical starting point.

evidence.note: The video establishes its medieval theme and introduces Montgomery's illustrated history of warfare.

segments.title: Norman cavalry, fortifications, and crusading expansion
segments.summary: A reading on Norman warfare links heavy cavalry and strategic fortification to expansion in England, southern Italy, and the Crusades.
segments.body: Viking armies had relied on infantry, while their Norman descendants became known for heavy cavalry and strategic fortification. Norman expansion in the eleventh century established rule in England and southern Italy, followed by consolidation in the twelfth. Montgomery connects this military energy to the revival that produced the Crusades and stresses the Normans' appetite for war. He also brings in his family's Norman origins, Roger of Montgomery at Hastings, and his own army's movement through Normandy in the opposite direction in 1944.

evidence.note: The reading describes Norman heavy cavalry, fortification, territorial expansion, and involvement in the Crusades.

segments.title: Feudal armies and the military transition at Hastings
segments.summary: Montgomery's account uses Hastings to contrast balanced forces with feudal military organization and the prestige of the mounted knight.
segments.body: Feudal society did not readily produce balanced, all-arms armies like those of the Eastern Roman Empire. From Hastings until the resurgence of Swiss and English infantry in the fourteenth century, the mounted knight held the prestige of the ideal soldier. Crusading armies differed from ordinary feudal levies because they attracted more volunteers, yet their mixture of peoples and rival leaders also made them less coherent. The comparison separates battlefield reputation from the institutional ability to coordinate cavalry, infantry, and other arms.

evidence.note: The reading compares feudal forces, Eastern Roman combined arms, mounted knights, and mixed crusading armies.

segments.title: William's command experience before the conquest of England
segments.summary: Montgomery presents William as a seasoned ruler, tactician, and strategist before the invasion of 1066.
segments.body: Montgomery pauses before the invasion narrative to assess William as an experienced commander rather than an untested adventurer. By 1066, William had ruled for thirty-one years through baronial revolts and the conquest of Maine. The account credits him with tactical skill but places still more weight on strategy, ruses, patience, and mastery of men. The Channel crossing follows decades of political survival and military experience.

evidence.note: The reading describes William's long rule, earlier campaigns, tactical reputation, strategic resourcefulness, and leadership.

segments.title: Channel patrols and mobilization before the Norman invasion
segments.summary: The 1066 campaign pits a prepared cross-Channel invasion against seasonal naval patrols, the fyrd, thegns, and professional housecarls.
segments.body: William's invasion appears as a long-prepared expansion rather than a sudden raid, supported by months of preparation and propaganda. Harold must cover threats from both Normandy and Norway, so England's limited naval strength patrols between Dover and the Isle of Wight through the summer. The fyrd supplies the army's main mass at a rate of one man for every six hundred acres, but its two-month service obligation makes prolonged readiness difficult. Thegns rank above ordinary freemen and below the aristocracy, owing military service directly to the king. The English army fights on foot with spears, javelins, swords, and large Danish axes, while wealthier men wear helmets and mail. Professional housecarls provide the household military core, with the discussion dividing them between archers and large axemen. Naval warning and the limits of seasonal service shape England's response before Hastings.

evidence.note: The transcript covers William's preparations, Harold's Channel patrols, fyrd service limits, and housecarls.

segments.title: Acre, Venice, and the maritime foundations of crusader power
segments.summary: Dan Jones's history shows how Acre's protected harbour, Venetian shipping, and colonial privileges sustained the Latin East.
segments.body: Acre is presented as a commercial and logistical hub linking the Latin states to pilgrims and merchants arriving by land and sea. The kings of Jerusalem claim direct rule over the city instead of granting it as a feudal holding, and Acre ranks with Jaffa as a main port of entry. Artificial harbour walls shelter shipping, while a heavy chain across the entrance protects it from hostile vessels. Venetian sailors receive extensive privileges after helping conquer Tyre, including a self-governing colony and the right to live by their own customs. Baldwin II also has reason to remain on good terms with a fleet that has sacked Byzantine towns, attacked Rhodes, and taken relics from Chios. Those concessions tie Venetian commercial interests to the survival of the crusader states and create an overseas source of military support. The charter's witnesses include Hugh of Payns, the founding master of the Templars.

evidence.note: The reading describes Acre's harbour defences, Venetian naval assistance, colonial privileges, and the Templars.

segments.title: The Mediterranean as a framework for medieval history
segments.summary: The third book treats Mediterranean connections as essential to medieval European history and to long-distance trade.
segments.body: John Julius Norwich's The Middle Sea provides the third selection. The introduction uses it to argue that medieval Europe cannot be understood apart from the Mediterranean. Even a history centered on China would encounter the sea through the spice trade. The book supplies the setting for the Sicilian, Genoese, papal, crusader, and Mamluk material that follows.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke connects medieval European history and the wider spice trade to the Mediterranean.

segments.title: The Sicilian Vespers becomes a Mediterranean power struggle
segments.summary: A Mediterranean history traces how Sicily drew France, Aragon, Genoa, and the papacy into a conflict that distracted attention from the crusader states.
segments.body: The War of the Sicilian Vespers continues into the next century because France, the papacy, Aragon, and Genoa all have stakes in the struggle for Sicily. Family honor commits Philip III and Philip IV to recovering the island for Charles, while the papacy has its own prestige invested in its grant and declares a crusade against Aragon. Diplomatic missions carry the dispute across Europe until most Mediterranean powers are involved. The Mamluks remain outside that contest, concentrating on the destruction of the crusader states. Western rulers are deeply engaged in Mediterranean politics while offering the Latin East no effective reinforcement.

evidence.note: The passage links the Sicilian Vespers to French, Aragonese, Genoese, papal, and Mamluk strategic interests.

segments.title: Mongol diplomacy seeks a western alliance for the Holy Land
segments.summary: Mongol embassies propose coordinated action against the Mamluks, but sympathetic European courts offer no firm armies or timetable.
segments.body: Arghun's envoys travel among papal, French, and English courts seeking practical support for the threatened crusader states. They receive elaborate welcomes and sympathetic hearings, but no ruler supplies a definite force or timetable. A later proposal offers twenty to thirty thousand Mongol horsemen for a coordinated advance toward Damascus and promises to return the Holy Places if western armies join. Even that specific plan produces no binding commitment, and repeated embassies fail before Arghun's death. The embassies travel widely, but they cannot turn sympathy into coalition warfare after European crusading enthusiasm has faded.

evidence.note: The reading recounts Mongol embassies and an unsuccessful proposal for coordinated armies to recover the Holy Places.

segments.title: Tripoli, Acre, and the failure of maritime relief
segments.summary: The destruction of Tripoli prompts a Venetian-led galley response, but disorder at Acre helps end the truce before a much larger Mamluk army arrives.
segments.body: When the Mamluks storm Tripoli, the account says that Christian men are killed, women and children enslaved, and the city burned. Venice then sends twenty war galleys, and Aragon adds five more to protect Christian interests at Acre. The fleet brings naval force along with poorly controlled adventurers from northern Italy. Their attack on Muslim residents destroys the remaining truce and hardens the sultan's decision to eliminate the Frankish enclave. The Mamluk army that follows is described in exaggerated numbers, yet it still plainly dwarfs Acre's few hundred knights and roughly fourteen thousand foot soldiers. Maritime reinforcement, indiscipline ashore, and a severe force imbalance converge in the final crisis of the crusader states.

evidence.note: The transcript covers Tripoli's fall, the Venetian and Aragonese galley force, violence at Acre, and the Mamluk advance.

segments.title: Richard II's French truce becomes an English political liability
segments.summary: The comic history links profitable English soldiering to the hostility that met Richard II's French marriage and truce.
segments.body: Stephen Clarke's irreverent account treats late-fourteenth-century campaigning as an economic opportunity for English soldiers crossing the Channel. Against that culture, Richard II's 1396 marriage to the French king's young daughter and his 1398 truce with France looked like appeasement to frustrated interests at home. The author presents Richard's reputation as a Francophile as one contributing factor in his deposition in 1399, not as a complete explanation. Peace policy, dynastic marriage, and the incentives of military labour could all become entangled with royal legitimacy.

evidence.note: The reading links profitable campaigning, Richard II's French marriage and truce, domestic criticism, and his deposition.

segments.title: French civil war gives England diplomatic leverage
segments.summary: Charles VI's incapacity and the Burgundian-Armagnac struggle let English forces trade intervention for money and territory.
segments.body: Charles VI's recurring incapacity leaves Burgundian and Armagnac factions fighting for control of France. Their rivalry brings atrocities against French communities, making the conflict more than a court quarrel. English forces can sell support to one side and then switch when the other offers more money or territory. Henry V's 1414 agreement with the Armagnacs consequently restores English holdings in southwestern France before his invasion. French fragmentation gives the English king both diplomatic and military leverage.

evidence.note: The reading covers Charles VI's incapacity, Burgundian-Armagnac violence, English military bargaining, and Henry V's treaty.

segments.title: Henry V builds warrior kingship before invading France
segments.summary: Henry enters the 1415 campaign with battlefield experience, a claim to France, strong religious conviction, and a year of military preparation behind him.
segments.body: Henry V inherits the throne at twenty-six, surrounded by eligible male relatives and under pressure to demonstrate strength. His cropped hair, reported ease in armour, and scar from an arrow wound sustained in Wales contribute to the image of a warrior king. The account also treats his religious conviction as central to his belief that he should rule France. When French factions seek English support, Henry demands a royal marriage and the French crown, then cites their refusal as a reason for war. He has already spent a year recruiting troops and manufacturing cannon, so the diplomatic quarrel supplies a public justification for preparations already in progress.

evidence.note: The reading describes Henry V's martial image, early wound, religious conviction, dynastic demands, and advance military preparations.

segments.title: Henry V's invasion fleet lands at Harfleur
segments.summary: The 1415 invasion uses a vast Solent fleet to carry soldiers, animals, artillery, and supplies to the Seine estuary at Harfleur.
segments.body: Henry chooses a Normandy landing rather than the familiar route through Calais and assembles a fleet described as roughly 1,500 ships. The vessels carry more than ten thousand fighters along with horses, cattle, cannon, and the supplies needed to sustain an invasion army. His 540-ton flagship Trinity Royal sails from the Solent amid banners and heraldic display, making the voyage a political spectacle as well as a transport operation. The force lands near the Seine estuary at Harfleur, where the fleet's scale turns unloading into a two-day task. The figures make the material demands of a major medieval amphibious operation unusually concrete.

evidence.note: The passage details the fleet's route, size, cargo, flagship, landing, and two-day unloading effort.

segments.title: Henry V imposes discipline after the Harfleur landing
segments.summary: After unloading, Henry forbids looting, massacre, and rape, imposing limits on how the invasion army may behave ashore.
segments.body: Henry waits until the whole army has disembarked before announcing rules for its conduct in Normandy. He forbids looting, massacre, and rape. The comic account immediately adds that killing Frenchmen remains permitted, so the orders regulate violence rather than end it. Issuing them after the two-day unloading establishes the terms under which a very large transported force will operate ashore.

evidence.note: The reading recounts Henry's post-landing prohibitions on looting, massacre, and rape, alongside the campaign's continued violence.

segments.title: Harfleur's defences and disease break Henry's invasion plan
segments.summary: Harfleur's strong defences, dysentery, occupation demands, and garrison needs cost Henry the force required to advance on Paris.
segments.body: Harfleur's strengthened defences turn an expected capture into a siege lasting until 22 September. English losses come from cannon and crossbow fire but especially from disease, identified as probably dysentery. After the surrender, Henry takes valuable hostages, spares poorer inhabitants, allows some to remain, and reallocates elite houses to English occupants. With roughly a third of his army dead and more soldiers evacuated sick or retained as a garrison, the planned advance on Paris becomes impossible. Disease, garrison demands, and occupation choices undo the invasion timetable even after a military victory.

evidence.note: The reading covers Harfleur's defences, dysentery, surrender terms, English losses, garrison needs, and the abandoned advance on Paris.

segments.title: Blocked crossings turn the Calais march toward Agincourt
segments.summary: Rain, destroyed crossings, a long inland detour, and a larger French army leave Henry's exhausted force facing battle near Agincourt.
segments.body: Henry turns toward Calais expecting a manageable march through countryside already damaged by earlier English raids. Torrential rain and French blocking forces instead make one river crossing after another unusable, forcing his army to fight at bridges and fords and detour about seventy kilometres inland before crossing the Somme. Supplies, troop condition, and morale fall together as the French army moves to cut off the retreat. The account rejects Shakespeare's figure of sixty thousand French troops but still estimates a force of twenty to thirty thousand, at least four times larger than Henry's exhausted army. When French messengers announce battle, Henry answers that events will follow God's will. That night, his men camp in mud, see French fires stretching across the horizon, and prepare to die before Agincourt. Failed movement and supply have created the crisis before the battle begins.

evidence.note: The reading covers rain, blocked bridges and fords, the Somme detour, collapsing supplies and morale, French numbers, and the approach to Agincourt.
